old: **The denominator matters.** Parking beeps, rear/360° views, automatic parking, low-speed emergency braking, remote parking and driverless valet/robotaxi docking are related but different products. The first two are familiar, cost-sensitive passenger-car functions; the last two can demand a fuller, safety-critical 3D surround view. A forecast that short-range flash/e-scan (electronically scanned) units become a large *share of automotive lidar units* (§F5) says nothing by itself about their share of **all parking sensors**. This report has no verified global installation series or matched system-price series for parking lidar, so I do not assign it a market-size number.

Driverless valet, robotaxi docking and commercial vehicles have a stronger case, because the machine, rather than a watching driver, must resolve small obstacles and blind zones [E]. These are **product hypotheses**, not verified adoption forecasts.

old: - **Lateral sampling.** A single wide acoustic beam has little angle information, although multiple sensors and vehicle motion can help localization. Radar lateral performance depends strongly on antenna aperture, angular processing, multipath (echoes arriving by more than one path) and near-field calibration, so no one 12- or 48-channel figure represents all parking radars. The FT120 figures follow from its 0.625° grid (160 × 120 over 100° × 75°); the FTX's 492k pts/s at 10 Hz fits a 256 × 192 grid, i.e. ≈0.55° (140° × 105°) to ≈0.7° (180° × 140°). In a high-resolution fisheye camera image, millimetre pixel spacing at 1 m does not establish metric depth accuracy or coverage at the bumper.

old: - **Exports carry Chinese lidar.** Chinese vans sold abroad fit RoboSense or Hesai units. In the US they would meet the Chinese-lidar and connected-vehicle restrictions (§D3); whether those rules cover delivery vehicles is not confirmed [U].
new: - **Exports carry Chinese lidar.** Chinese vans sold abroad fit RoboSense or Hesai units. In the US the barrier is the van, not its lidar. The Commerce Department's [connected-vehicle rule](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2025-01-16/pdf/2025-00592.pdf) (15 CFR 791 subpart D, §D3) covers road vehicles of up to 10,000 lb gross vehicle weight; for vans in that class it bars China-controlled makers such as Neolix or Zelos, from model year 2027, from selling them in the US or running a commercial driverless service with them, and bars any importer from selling vans that run Chinese driving software [P]. The rule exempts lidar as automotive sensing and excludes sidewalk delivery robots [P]. Since 28 Jul 2026, however, foreign-made autonomous mobile robots are on the FCC's Covered List, which blocks equipment authorization for new models, delivery robots included [P, FCC DA 26-786; I for delivery robots]. The Pentagon's lidar bans reach only what the Defense Department buys and operates (§D3), and a van without manual controls also needs an NHTSA exemption from the federal safety standards, as Nuro's R2 received in 2020 [P, 85 FR 7826].
